title: Intrauterine Contraception: Eligibility, Safe Insertion, and Problem-Focused Follow-Up
bottomLine: Intrauterine contraception is highly effective and appropriate for many adolescents, nulliparous patients and postpartum patients. Confirm pregnancy is reasonably excluded, assess infection/anatomic issues that actually affect insertion, choose copper versus levonorgestrel IUC by goals and contraindications, and investigate pain, bleeding, pregnancy symptoms or missing strings according to the clinical problem rather than scheduling unnecessary routine procedures.
recognize: Copper IUC provides hormone-free long-term contraception; levonorgestrel systems reduce bleeding for many users.
Nulliparity and adolescence are not contraindications by themselves.
differentiate: Current purulent cervicitis/untreated gonorrhea or chlamydia changes insertion timing; remote STI history alone does not prohibit IUC use.
Expected early cramping/spotting differs from severe pain, fever, pregnancy symptoms or heavy bleeding that raises expulsion, perforation, infection or ectopic-pregnancy concern.
assessment: Clarify contraceptive goals, pregnancy possibility, recent unprotected intercourse, bleeding pattern, STI risk/symptoms, uterine/anatomic history and preferences around hormones/menstrual effects.
workup: Use pregnancy testing and STI testing according to timing/risk without creating unnecessary insertion delays when same-day care is safe under the current pathway.
Missing strings require pregnancy assessment and localization rather than blind instrumentation.
management: Provide informed choice, aseptic insertion and immediate complication assessment according to local scope/training.
Manage expected bleeding/cramping conservatively; evaluate suspected expulsion, perforation, pregnancy or infection promptly.
Removal should be timely and patient-directed when requested; difficult/nonvisible-string removals require appropriate expertise.
medicationSafety: Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for every insertion.
If pregnancy occurs with an IUC, promptly assess location because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded; removal decisions depend on string/access and pregnancy goals.
redFlags: Severe or escalating pelvic pain after insertion
counselling: Discuss expected bleeding changes, efficacy, STI protection limitations, how to seek help for warning symptoms and that removal is available whenever desired.
followUp: Routine mandatory string-check visits are not required for every asymptomatic user; follow up for symptoms, concerns, difficult insertion or local policy indications.
examTrap: Treating adolescence/nulliparity as a contraindication—or delaying a safe insertion for STI test results in an asymptomatic patient when testing can be performed at insertion under the current pathway.
oneLinePearl: IUC care is eligibility plus informed choice plus symptom-triggered follow-up—not parity-based gatekeeping.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada contraception resources and current IUC statements

title: Contraceptive Implant: Expected Bleeding, Drug Interactions, and Safe Removal
bottomLine: The etonogestrel implant is a highly effective progestin-only contraceptive. Counsel before placement that irregular bleeding is common, assess enzyme-inducing drug interactions and pregnancy timing, and manage bleeding or removal requests without pressuring the patient to continue a method they no longer want.
recognize: Unpredictable spotting, prolonged bleeding or amenorrhea can all occur and do not by themselves mean reduced contraceptive efficacy.
The implant is suitable for many patients who cannot use estrogen.
differentiate: New heavy bleeding, pelvic pain or pregnancy symptoms require evaluation for another cause rather than automatic attribution to the implant.
Strong hepatic enzyme inducers can reduce implant effectiveness and require an alternative/additional contraceptive strategy.
assessment: Review pregnancy possibility, bleeding history, medications/herbals, liver disease, breast-cancer history and reproductive goals.
workup: Investigate pregnancy, anemia, infection or structural bleeding causes when the clinical pattern warrants it; routine imaging is not needed when the implant is readily palpable and functioning.
management: Use evidence-based short-term strategies for bothersome bleeding when appropriate and desired, while offering removal at any time.
Nonpalpable/deep implants require localization and experienced removal rather than blind exploration.
medicationSafety: Review enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs, rifamycins and other relevant interactions.
Do not repeatedly expose a patient to estrogen/NSAID treatment for bleeding without reviewing contraindications and whether they simply prefer removal.
counselling: Set realistic bleeding expectations and explain that troublesome bleeding is treatable but removal remains the patient's choice.
followUp: Reassess bleeding, interaction changes and patient satisfaction; confirm complete removal when removal is performed.
examTrap: Calling irregular bleeding 'treatment failure'—or refusing requested removal because the implant remains medically effective.
oneLinePearl: Implant success includes contraceptive efficacy, bleeding tolerability and patient control over continuation.
sourceBasis: SOGC 2025 position statements on contraceptive implant removal and progestin-only contraceptive bleeding

title: Oral Contraception: Match Estrogen Risk, Adherence, and Reproductive Goals
bottomLine: Choose combined versus progestin-only oral contraception from medical eligibility, thrombosis/vascular risk, medication interactions, bleeding preferences and adherence needs. A pelvic exam is not required merely to prescribe pills, but blood pressure and a focused contraindication history matter before estrogen-containing contraception.
recognize: Combined hormonal contraception can improve cycle control and dysmenorrhea but adds estrogen-related thrombotic/vascular risk.
Progestin-only pills are useful when estrogen is unsuitable but adherence/timing characteristics differ by product.
differentiate: Migraine with aura, major VTE/thrombophilia risk, certain cardiovascular disease, severe uncontrolled hypertension and some smoking/age combinations can make estrogen-containing contraception unsafe.
Common breakthrough bleeding/nausea differs from symptoms concerning for VTE, stroke or pregnancy.
assessment: Measure BP and review migraine aura, VTE history, smoking/nicotine, cardiovascular disease, postpartum status, liver/breast disease, medications/herbals and adherence preferences.
workup: Pregnancy testing is guided by timing/possibility; routine thrombophilia screening, pelvic examination or laboratory panels are not required before pills in an otherwise appropriate patient.
management: Use the safest effective formulation consistent with preferences and current Canadian eligibility guidance.
Address adherence, missed pills and backup/emergency contraception using the specific product instructions rather than one rule for all pills.
medicationSafety: Review enzyme-inducing drugs that can reduce efficacy.
New severe headache/focal neurologic symptoms, chest pain/dyspnea or unilateral leg swelling require urgent thrombotic/vascular assessment rather than routine pill follow-up.
counselling: Discuss benefits, common bleeding effects, STI protection limitations and a missed-pill plan using the exact formulation.
followUp: Recheck BP and tolerability at clinically appropriate intervals and whenever cardiovascular risk or medications change.
examTrap: Ordering pelvic exam/thrombophilia labs for every pill start—or prescribing estrogen without asking about migraine aura and VTE risk.
oneLinePearl: For oral contraception, the key pre-prescribing tests are history, blood pressure and pregnancy timing—not a routine pelvic exam.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada contraception guidance

title: Emergency Contraception: Act on Timing and Ongoing Pregnancy Risk
bottomLine: Emergency contraception is time-sensitive and should be offered after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure without unnecessary examination or testing delays. Choose the most effective feasible option for timing, body/medication factors and patient preference, then establish ongoing contraception and pregnancy follow-up.
recognize: Copper IUC is a highly effective emergency-contraception option and provides ongoing contraception.
Oral emergency-contraception effectiveness depends on timing and product; ongoing intercourse after the dose creates new pregnancy risk.
differentiate: Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy before implantation and does not terminate an established pregnancy.
It does not protect against STIs and does not replace evaluation after sexual assault or coercion when applicable.
assessment: Clarify intercourse dates, cycle/pregnancy possibility, current contraception, medications including enzyme inducers, IUC eligibility and reproductive goals.
workup: Do not require pregnancy testing before EC when it would delay treatment and established pregnancy is not suspected; arrange follow-up testing based on timing and subsequent menses/symptoms.
management: Offer copper IUC or oral EC according to current Canadian guidance and availability; do not withhold because the patient may have had other unprotected intercourse without discussing the appropriate pathway.
Provide a clear plan for starting/resuming ongoing contraception because timing differs after different oral EC products.
medicationSafety: Enzyme-inducing medications can reduce oral EC effectiveness and may favour a non-interacting option.
Do not advise taking conflicting hormonal regimens without accounting for the chosen EC product's mechanism and restart interval.
redFlags: Sexual assault/coercion requiring urgent comprehensive care
Severe abdominal pain after subsequent pregnancy concern
counselling: Explain expected bleeding changes, pregnancy-test timing, STI considerations and ongoing contraception options without judgment.
followUp: Confirm pregnancy status if the expected menses does not occur and ensure ongoing contraception access.
examTrap: Delaying EC for a pelvic exam or routine laboratory testing until the time-sensitive window narrows.
oneLinePearl: Emergency contraception is a clock: treat first, then close the loop on ongoing contraception and pregnancy testing.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada contraception resources

title: Preconception Care: Optimize Health Before Embryogenesis Begins
bottomLine: Preconception care identifies modifiable medical, medication, nutritional, infectious, genetic and social risks before pregnancy, when changes can prevent early fetal exposure and improve fertility/pregnancy outcomes. Start with reproductive goals and patient priorities rather than assuming pregnancy intention.
recognize: Diabetes, hypertension, thyroid/autoimmune disease, epilepsy, obesity, mental health/substance use and teratogenic medications can materially change pregnancy planning.
Rubella/varicella and other vaccine status matters because selected live vaccines must be given before pregnancy rather than during pregnancy.
differentiate: Routine preconception counselling differs from infertility evaluation and from prenatal care after pregnancy is established.
Folic-acid needs are risk-specific; not every patient requires the same high-dose regimen.
assessment: Ask whether and when pregnancy is desired, chronic disease control, medications/supplements, immunization/STI risk, prior pregnancy outcomes, genetic/family history, nutrition, substance exposure, mental health, IPV and social/access barriers.
workup: Use disease/risk-directed labs, immunity or carrier/genetic testing; avoid indiscriminate panels without a clinical indication.
management: Optimize chronic disease before conception, replace contraindicated medications safely rather than abruptly stopping needed therapy, provide risk-appropriate folic-acid guidance and update immunizations.
Refer genetics, maternal-fetal medicine or disease specialists when risk requires it.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, valproate and other known pregnancy-risk medications require indication-specific preconception review and safer alternatives where possible.
Do not stop essential psychiatric/neurologic therapy abruptly solely because pregnancy is planned; balance relapse and fetal risks.
redFlags: Current teratogenic medication without a safe transition plan
counselling: Use inclusive, non-stigmatizing counselling about nutrition, activity, age-related fertility, substances and reproductive timing.
followUp: Confirm medication/vaccine/chronic-disease changes are completed and arrange timely pregnancy/infertility follow-up based on goals.
examTrap: Waiting until the first prenatal visit to review teratogenic medications, diabetes control or live-vaccine needs.
oneLinePearl: Preconception care moves preventable risk reduction to before the pregnancy test turns positive.
sourceBasis: SOGC Preconception Health Hub and current preconception guidance
Public Health Agency of Canada preconception resources

title: Infertility: Evaluate Ovulation, Anatomy, and Sperm in Parallel
bottomLine: Initial infertility evaluation should assess the major contributors in parallel—ovulation, uterine/tubal anatomy and sperm—while timing referral earlier for advanced reproductive age, amenorrhea, known tubal disease, severe male-factor risk or other clear fertility threats. Do not make one partner complete an exhaustive workup before evaluating the other.
recognize: Irregular/absent menses suggests ovulatory dysfunction; prior PID/ectopic/endometriosis/surgery raises tubal risk; testicular disease, chemotherapy or sexual dysfunction raises male-factor risk.
differentiate: Infertility is not synonymous with anovulation or PCOS; age-related ovarian reserve, tubal disease, endometriosis and sperm factors are common alternatives/cofactors.
assessment: Clarify duration/frequency/timing of intercourse or insemination, menstrual/ovulatory pattern, pregnancies/losses, pelvic infection/surgery, endometriosis symptoms, medications/substances, age and goals; obtain semen-factor history concurrently.
workup: Use pregnancy/TSH/prolactin or other endocrine testing when clinically indicated, document ovulation when uncertain, obtain semen analysis early and assess tubal/uterine anatomy according to history and referral pathway.
Ovarian-reserve tests estimate response to stimulation better than they predict spontaneous fertility in isolation.
management: Treat reversible contributors and refer to fertility/reproductive endocrinology according to duration, age and high-risk features rather than applying one waiting period to everyone.
medicationSafety: Ovulation-induction medications require diagnosis-specific monitoring and multiple-gestation/ovarian-response safety; do not empirically prescribe them before completing basic evaluation.
counselling: Use non-blaming language and explain that infertility commonly has more than one contributor.
followUp: Close the loop on semen/anatomic/endocrine results and ensure age-sensitive referral is not delayed by serial low-value tests.
examTrap: Ordering months of endocrine testing for one partner before obtaining a basic semen analysis and reproductive history from both contributors.
oneLinePearl: Infertility workup is parallel: ovulation, anatomy and sperm—not a one-partner obstacle course.
sourceBasis: SOGC fertility and advanced reproductive age guidance

title: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency: Confirm the Diagnosis and Replace Lost Ovarian Health
bottomLine: Suspect premature ovarian insufficiency in a patient under 40 with persistent menstrual disturbance/amenorrhea and hypoestrogenic features after pregnancy and other causes are considered. Confirm biochemically through the current POI pathway, evaluate selected autoimmune/genetic causes, address fertility and bone/cardiovascular/sexual health, and replace estrogen when appropriate until the usual menopause age rather than treating symptoms alone.
recognize: Irregular/absent menses, hot flashes, vaginal dryness and infertility can occur, but intermittent ovarian activity/pregnancy remains possible.
POI has long-term bone and cardiovascular implications beyond fertility.
differentiate: Pregnancy, hypothalamic amenorrhea, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease and PCOS are important alternatives.
POI differs from natural menopause because intermittent ovarian activity can occur and health consequences arise decades earlier.
assessment: Assess menstrual timeline, pregnancy possibility, vasomotor/genitourinary symptoms, weight/exercise/eating pattern, galactorrhea, autoimmune symptoms, chemo/radiation/surgery and family/genetic history.
workup: Use pregnancy testing, FSH confirmation according to current POI guidance, and thyroid/prolactin or cause-directed autoimmune/genetic evaluation when indicated.
Assess bone health and cardiovascular risk according to age/duration/risk.
management: Offer physiologic hormone replacement when not contraindicated through approximately the usual menopause age, individualized to uterine status and risk.
Refer for fertility counselling because spontaneous ovulation may occur but donor-oocyte/other fertility options may be relevant.
medicationSafety: Hormone replacement for POI has a different benefit-risk context from initiating menopausal hormone therapy at older age; do not withhold needed replacement solely by extrapolating older-menopause risks.
If the uterus is present, systemic estrogen requires adequate endometrial protection.
redFlags: Contraindication to systemic hormone requiring specialist plan
counselling: Discuss fertility uncertainty, bone/heart health, sexual symptoms and psychological impact; use the patient's preferred reproductive goals.
followUp: Track symptoms, bleeding, bone/cardiovascular health and hormone tolerability/adherence.
examTrap: Treating a 32-year-old with POI like a 55-year-old starting optional menopausal symptom therapy and withholding replacement without considering decades of estrogen deficiency.
oneLinePearl: POI is early loss of ovarian endocrine function, so management protects long-term health as well as symptoms.
sourceBasis: ESHRE 2024 POI guideline referenced by Canadian Menopause Society

title: Pelvic Floor Disorders: Identify Prolapse, Incontinence, Pain, and Functional Impact
bottomLine: Pelvic-floor disorders are symptom-and-function diagnoses that include pelvic organ prolapse, urinary/fecal incontinence and pelvic-floor muscle dysfunction. Clarify which function is impaired, examine when appropriate, address reversible contributors and offer conservative pelvic-floor therapy before assuming every patient needs surgery.
recognize: Vaginal pressure/bulge, incomplete emptying, stress/urge leakage, fecal leakage and pelvic-floor pain can coexist.
Pregnancy/vaginal birth, aging, obesity, chronic cough/constipation and connective-tissue factors can increase risk.
differentiate: Stress and urgency incontinence require different first-line strategies; urinary retention, fistula or neurologic bladder are separate problems.
Pelvic pain is not always caused by a weak pelvic floor—overactivity/myofascial dysfunction can require down-training rather than strengthening.
assessment: Ask bulge/pressure, urinary/fecal symptoms, voiding/defecation, pain/sexual function, obstetric/surgical history, constipation/cough, neurologic symptoms and patient goals.
workup: Use focused pelvic examination, urinalysis/postvoid residual or bladder diary when clinically indicated; reserve advanced urodynamics/imaging for complex or preprocedural questions.
management: Treat constipation/cough and offer pelvic-floor physiotherapy, bladder/bowel retraining, pessary or other conservative options according to the disorder and goals.
Refer urogynecology/urology/colorectal/pelvic-floor specialists for significant prolapse, retention, refractory symptoms, fistula or surgical consideration.
medicationSafety: Antimuscarinic/other bladder medications require cognitive, constipation, glaucoma and retention risk review.
Do not prescribe strengthening Kegels reflexively for pain caused by an overactive pelvic floor.
redFlags: New saddle anesthesia/leg weakness/bowel-bladder neurologic change
counselling: Normalize discussion of pelvic-floor symptoms and explain that conservative options can meaningfully improve function.
followUp: Track symptom/function goals and reassess after physiotherapy/pessary/behavioural or medication interventions.
examTrap: Prescribing pelvic-floor strengthening to every patient with pelvic pain without determining whether the muscles are weak or overactive.
oneLinePearl: Pelvic-floor treatment follows the function that is failing—not one universal exercise prescription.
sourceBasis: Canadian pelvic-health physiotherapy and urogynecology principles
